\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling---repeated sampling with self-consistency or best-of-$N$---yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning, but whether these gains transfer to NER remains open.
We characterize when scaling succeeds and fails, using NER (four datasets, primarily 7--14B fine-tuned) as the primary case study with preliminary RE and SQL pilots.
Quality estimation signals predict output quality (AUROC up to $0.82$), yet instance-level selection yields ${<}1$\,pp, revealing a \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
A diagnostic framework identifies two co-occurring conditions---\textit{degeneracy} (i.e., multiple outputs collapsing to identical predictions) and signal alignment collapse---that jointly determine scaling returns; cross-task exploration confirms task-specific failure modes.
Entity-level construction provides statistically significant conditional gains ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, 3-epoch; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$; diminishes at convergence) but exhibits inverse scaling in most configurations (69\% of $N$-transitions), underscoring the framework's diagnostic value over prescriptive remedy.
The framework is diagnostic rather than predictive, informing resource allocation decisions before investing in repeated inference.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling---self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}, extended reasoning \cite{muennighoff2025s1}---yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks where outputs admit equivalence classes or execution-based verification.
For NER, where outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, the boundary conditions for effective scaling are unknown; prior work \cite{yao2026consistency, yun2025price} provides initial observations but no systematic diagnostic framework quantifying failure mechanisms at entity level across multiple model families.
While \citet{yao2026consistency} demonstrate that scaling returns plateau at the task level, our contribution operates at a different granularity: instance-level diagnostic decomposition revealing \emph{why} specific instances resist scaling (degeneracy $+$ LP compression), with actionable per-instance signals.

Using NER (four datasets, primarily 7--14B fine-tuned; tentative cross-scale observations to 72B) and RE as case studies, we identify a \textbf{correlation-selection gap}: quality estimation signals predict output quality ($\rho$ up to $0.45$, AUROC $0.82$; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}), yet selection fails---MV gains ${<}1$\,pp even at $N{=}64$ (Figure~\ref{fig:n_scaling}; Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
This gap decomposes into a definitional layer---four instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates---and an empirical one: LP, the only per-sample signal, also fails through within-instance compression (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
A hidden-state probe confirms models encode entity quality internally (AUROC $0.63$\textendash$0.88$; Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic}), exposing an \textit{introspection boundary} \cite{huang2024large}.
A \textit{diagnostic framework}---co-occurring conditions that jointly characterize the gap, not a sequential filter---localizes the failure to degeneracy ($12$--$68$\%) and signal alignment collapse ($\alpha{\to}0$), which jointly prevent selection (Table~\ref{tab:method_summary}).
Our framework is \emph{diagnostic}: it decomposes observed failures post-hoc rather than predicting which instances will fail a priori (predictive extension remains future work).
The optimal strategy is dataset-dependent (LP $+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD; MV $+0.61$\,pp on CoNLL), and RE reveals a distinct bottleneck ($40$\% zero-F1; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
Entity-level construction provides statistically significant conditional improvement ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, 3-epoch; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$; diminishes at convergence) where the framework predicts success---low degeneracy and LP-F1 alignment---but inverse scaling in 69\% of $N$-transitions confirms that scaling is harmful in most configurations.

We quantify a well-known capability-diversity tradeoff \cite{yun2025price} in the NER context: degeneracy rises with model capability, diminishing scaling returns across tested NER configurations.
These findings rest on four NER benchmarks, two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with 4B/14B ablations, $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 64\}$, and exploratory extensions to RE\footnote{RE F1 is confounded by entity span errors: the majority of zero-F1 RE instances reflect upstream NER mismatches rather than relation classification failure (Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).} and SQL parsing ($87.2$\% degeneracy).

\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

Our investigation proceeds in three stages:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Discover} [Empirical] (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}).
    QE signals achieve AUROC up to $0.82$; a hidden-state probe reveals an introspection boundary ($0.88$ vs.\ self-judgment $0.51$; Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnose} [Diagnostic] (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}).

The directional pattern is consistent.}
118	This sensitivity---favorable conditions are fragile and training-dependent---reinforces that Few-NERD is a conditional success rather than evidence of a general bypass. The core negative finding (selection ${\leq}$ greedy under high degeneracy) is unaffected.

1	\section{Discussion and Conclusion}\label{sec:discussion}\label{sec:selection_method}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Why test-time scaling fails for NER.}
4	For discrete-answer reasoning, sample diversity reflects diverse reasoning paths; for NER, degeneracy ($12$--$68$\%) eliminates candidate diversity while signal alignment collapse ($\alpha{\to}0$) prevents ranking.
5	The degeneracy decomposition (\S\ref{sec:theory}) identifies $\alpha$---not degeneracy---as the binding constraint ($8$--$33{\times}$ tighter), providing a diagnostic tool for localizing failure rather than a predictive bound.
6	This capability-diversity tradeoff \cite{yun2025price} persists across model families (5.5--74\%; Table~\ref{tab:frontier_sc_cross}), scales (4B--72B; \S\ref{sec:scaling}), and decoding modes (LP std ratio ${\approx}0.97{\times}$; \S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
7	Compared to \citet{yao2026consistency}'s task-level plateau, we provide instance-level decomposition; \citet{landesberg2026bon} independently confirm the gap generalizes beyond NER ($r{=}0.47$ global vs.\ $r{=}0.27$ within-prompt).
8	
9	\paragraph{Constrained vs.\ free-form decoding.}
10	LP compression is model-intrinsic rather than an artifact of constrained decoding: free-form generation yields nearly identical within-instance LP distributions (std ratio $0.97{\times}$; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}).
11	Constrained decoding does affect diversity: Few-NERD (13\% degeneracy) retains diversity under grammar constraints, while CoNLL (62\%) collapses---but this variation tracks task difficulty and model calibration rather than the decoding mechanism itself.
12	
13	\paragraph{Scale and outlook.}
14	The correlation-selection gap persists from 4B fine-tuned to 72B zero-shot and GPT-5.5, with degeneracy varying by model family rather than scale (Qwen2.5: $32$--$46$\%, Qwen3: $13$\%, GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:scaling}).
15	Whether models beyond 70B with improved calibration can overcome signal alignment collapse remains an open question; our diagnostic framework provides the measurements needed to evaluate this as larger models become available.
16	
17	\paragraph{Self-verification ruled out.}
18	We also test whether models can directly self-verify extracted entities via entailment prompting. Across three datasets, entailment-based self-judgment achieves near-random entity-level AUROC (0.50--0.55), while agreement-based signals reach 0.79--0.94 (Appendix~\ref{app:esj}), ruling out self-verification as an alternative to consistency-based quality estimation.
19	
20	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
21	Measuring degeneracy and LP-F1 alignment at $N{=}8$ suffices: if ${>}50$\% degenerate, scaling provides no benefit; if degeneracy ${<}20$\% with $\rho{>}0.70$, construction may yield gains; otherwise prefer greedy.
22	
23	\paragraph{Conclusion.}
24	The diagnostic framework---localizing failure to degeneracy and signal alignment collapse---is our primary contribution; RE, SQL, and cross-model extensions are exploratory.
25

\section{How Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}

The diagnostic framework (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
Probe experiments use Qwen2.5-7B (not the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B used in main experiments); conclusions are architecture-specific.
We evaluate self-verification and diagnostic probes on Qwen2.5-7B\footnote{ESJ, MRSC, and LSC use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (zero-shot self-verification capability) rather than the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B used in the main experiments. Conclusion direction is consistent with the main experiments' negative results across all fine-tuned selection strategies. The pattern---selection failure across all signals---is independently confirmed in the Qwen3-8B main experiments, making the introspection boundary a model-independent finding within our tested scale. Probe conclusions are limited to the Qwen2.5 architecture; linear probes may underestimate representational capacity (nonlinear alternatives are left to future work).} fine-tuned for NER on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
Following iterative self-refinement \cite{madaan2023selfrefine}, we re-prompt on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification; P(yes) separation between gold and non-gold entities is $0.0006$ ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.794$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) outperforms majority vote ($0.792$) but does not close the oracle gap ($0.882$).

\paragraph{Hidden-state probe.}
A logistic regression on mean-pooled final-layer hidden states at entity spans achieves AUROC $0.636$ (Few-NERD), $0.882$ (CoNLL), $0.630$ (SciERC), evaluated with GroupKFold CV (5-fold ${\times}$ 3 seeds, groups${=}$source instance to prevent entity-level leakage; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).
All three exceed ESJ ($0.51$); only CoNLL approaches frequency agreement ($0.868$).
Cross-dataset transfer is weak: leave-one-dataset-out AUROC drops to $0.559$ (Few-NERD${\to}$CoNLL) and $0.671$ (CoNLL${\to}$Few-NERD), indicating that entity error patterns are dataset-specific rather than reflecting a universal introspection boundary, limiting probe-based approaches without per-dataset calibration.
At the sample level, an MLP probe closes only 13.9\% of the oracle gap on SciERC (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).

\paragraph{The introspection boundary.}
Entity quality is partially encoded in hidden representations: a supervised probe (AUROC $0.63$\textendash$0.88$) consistently exceeds self-judgment (ESJ $0.51$) but only marginally exceeds multi-sample agreement ($0.87$) on CoNLL, suggesting consensus captures information beyond single-pass representations while the prompt interface fails to access even partial hidden-state signal.
LODO transfer drops to $0.56$\textendash$0.67$, so even direct hidden-state access would not yield a universal quality signal---consistent with the negative cross-dataset verifier transfer (\S\ref{sec:verifier}).

9	\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}
10	
11	Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
12	The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
13	Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).
14	
15	\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
16	Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
17	Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
18	Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).
19	
20	\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}
21	
22	\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
23	For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
24	where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
25	For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).
26	
27	\noindent The decomposition is diagnostic rather than predictive: the three factors ($D$, $G_{\textup{nd}}$, $\alpha$) localize where aggregation fails rather than forecasting performance.
28	Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound but it captures only 3--12\% of actual gains (Figure~\ref{fig:bound}): $\alpha$---not $D$---is the bottleneck ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$), and the bound cannot be tightened by signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) or verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}).
29	Conclusions are stable across $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$; signal alignment ($\alpha{\approx}0.068$) is the binding constraint, $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter than the degeneracy threshold.
30	
31	\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
32	The decomposition is an illustrative directional analysis showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative diagnostic tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.578$--$0.644$ reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.
33	
34	MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
35	Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.
